analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health insurance covering every U.S. resident, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and military health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced August 12, 1992 with zero cosponsors, it was split among seven House committees and five subcommittees and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a Canadian-style national health insurance system: every U.S. resident would be entitled to hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, mental health care, dental care, and long-term care, with the freedom to choose any participating provider. Medicare, Medicaid, CHAMPUS, and federal employee health benefits would be repealed and folded into the new program. It would be paid for by progressive premiums on individuals and by premiums on employers based on their size and profitability, and private insurance would be limited to supplemental coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident citizen, national, and lawful resident alien would be entitled to comprehensive health care and long-term care regardless of income or health status [S2]. People who are uninsured, underinsured, or lose coverage when they change jobs would gain guaranteed, portable coverage [S2]. Families would stop paying private premiums for core coverage, and no provider could bill a patient beyond the state program's payment (no balance billing) [S3]. Elderly and disabled people needing nursing home or home care would gain coverage without having to spend down their assets, since the bill requires cost sharing to be reduced so people can keep their homes and independence [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every U.S. resident citizen, national, and lawful resident alien to health care services and long-term care services, with automatic enrollment at birth or immigration and a state health insurance card [S2].

Covers inpatient and outpatient hospital care, emergency services, professional services including medically necessary dental care, preventive care, prescription drugs, substance abuse treatment, outpatient mental health, hospice, rehabilitation, and approved experimental treatment [S2].
Imposes no deductibles and no cost-sharing on preventive care, and requires states not to restrict timely access or permit life-threatening queues as a consequence of budget allocations [S3].
Makes payment by the state program payment in full: no individual would be liable for any amount for covered services, banning balance billing [S3].

Repeals Medicare, Medicaid, CHAMPUS, and federal employee health benefit provisions and consolidates their funding into a Federal Health Care Trust Fund, with 75-85% federal matching shares for the states [S2].

Finances the system through income-based, progressive individual premiums and employer premiums based on ability to pay, aiming to prevent an increase in the overall share of household health spending [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay premiums scaled to workforce size and profitability, and individuals would pay progressive income-based premiums [S2]. Employer group health plan expenses would no longer be tax-deductible unless the plan is the approved public program [S2]. Hospitals and other institutions would be paid from negotiated global operating, capital, and training budgets rather than billed per service, and practitioners would be paid from negotiated fee schedules designed to keep overall payments within the budget [S2]. Private insurers would lose most of their core market, retaining only supplemental or explicitly duplicative coverage with disclosure requirements [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces the entire employer-based insurance system and Medicare/Medicaid with a single public program — a massive transition whose financing (premiums on employers and a progressive premium on individuals, plus state financing programs) would fall heavily on employers and higher earners [S2].

Cost control relies on global hospital budgets and negotiated practitioner fee schedules intended to keep payments within budgeted amounts, a mechanism that can create pressure to limit service availability; the bill itself recognizes the risk by prohibiting queues with life-threatening potential, which suggests the tension was real [S2].

The Federal Health Board's regulations on services and cost-sharing would take effect automatically unless Congress passes a disapproval resolution within 60 days, shifting significant ongoing policy decisions from Congress to an appointed board [S3].

People satisfied with their current employer coverage would lose it, since employers could only deduct expenses for the approved public program, and private insurance would be confined to supplemental or duplicative options that do not relieve anyone of paying the public premium [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is very large: guaranteed comprehensive coverage — including long-term care, which almost no private policy covers adequately — for every resident, no deductibles, no balance billing, and portability across states. The costs are equally real: a large new financing structure on employers and individuals, the elimination of coverage arrangements many people liked, and a budgeted delivery system whose spending limits could strain access if set too low. The bill tried to blunt the biggest objections (freedom of provider choice, no life-threatening queues, supplemental private options allowed, malpractice reform grants), but it asked the country to abandon its entire health financing system at once — a lift that explains both the ambition and the political failure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1992, referred to seven House committees, farmed out to five subcommittees, and never reported out of any of them before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Andrews (D-ME) introduced the American Health Security Plan Act of 1992 in the House on August 12, 1992 [S1].
The bill was referred jointly to seven House committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Rules, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, and Post Office and Civil Service [S5].

Between August and October 1992 it was referred to five subcommittees, including the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health and the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations; no committee ever reported it [S5].
No vote was ever taken in the House or Senate, and the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, killing the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The employer-based private health insurance industry and the existing payment arrangements for hospitals and physicians were better off, because the system they operated in was never replaced. Millions of uninsured Americans remained without the guaranteed coverage the bill would have provided.

for.name: Rep. Thomas Andrews (D-ME)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it drew no cosponsors from either party [S4].

against.name: Chairs of the seven House committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill from any of the seven committees or five subcommittees to which it was referred [S5].

against.name: Private health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Fought single-payer proposals during the early-1990s health care debate, which the bill would have largely supplanted with a public program.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors — no Republican and no other Democrat signed on — and it received no action in the Democratic-controlled House [S4].

industries.note: The bill would repeal the tax treatment that supports employer-based private coverage and confine private insurance to supplemental or duplicative options, eliminating the industry's core market. Keeping the existing private system is what the industry's interest required, which ran against the bill's guaranteed public coverage [S2].

Institutions would be paid from global operating, capital, and training budgets negotiated with state boards — guaranteed revenue, but capped and allocated rather than billed per service. Ordinary people would gain access but rely on those budgets to fund timely care [S2].

Practitioners would get a universally insured patient population but face negotiated fee schedules designed to keep total payments within the health budget, capping income growth. Payment would be payment in full, with no patient balance billing [S2].

Employers would stop buying and administering private plans but would owe premiums based on workforce size and profitability, and lose the tax deduction for group health plans unless the plan is the approved public program. Businesses currently paying for coverage could gain predictability; those paying little would pay more [S2].
The bill covers nursing home, home- and community-based, and hospice care publicly, with income protections, removing the main reason families buy private long-term care policies [S3].
